1	# Task 10: Desert canyon at dusk with slow camera flythrough
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a desert canyon at dusk: tall layered sandstone walls on both sides of a winding dry riverbed, warm orange and magenta low sun near the horizon, a cool blue-violet sky gradient overhead, long soft shadows, and a few scattered boulders and dead shrubs on the canyon floor. Fine atmospheric haze should make distant walls fade toward the sky colour. The camera performs a slow, smooth, looping flythrough along the canyon floor at roughly eye height, gently drifting left and right, with no user input needed. Do not rely on any external image or model downloads; build everything procedurally or from assets the framework already provides. The page must show no console errors and must keep rendering continuously.
4	
5	The rendering contract in the next section applies.
6	
7	## Rendering contract (all tasks)
8	
9	- Draw into the existing `<canvas id="app">` (640x360 CSS pixels, device pixel ratio 1). Do not resize it or create another canvas.
10	- Render continuously with `requestAnimationFrame`. When the first frame has been drawn set `window.__EVAL_READY__ = true`.
11	- No network access: load assets only from `/assets/...` (served from `public/assets`). Do not import from CDNs.
12	- Code goes in `src/` (TypeScript, strict). The entry is `src/main.ts`. It must pass `typecheck

Since this will run in headless Chromium, I should keep the WebGL rendering fairly light. I'm sketching a canyon flythrough using a sine-based centerline path for the terrain, thinking about how to make the camera's journey loop smoothly by wrapping the z-position periodically.

To make the loop seamless, I'm working out a periodic height function with period P, building a terrain mesh that spans past the camera's travel range so fog hides the seam where it wraps. I'm leaning toward a terrain length around 500-900 units with a resolution that keeps vertex count manageable, and considering reusing a single periodic terrain segment as repeated copies rather than generating unique geometry for the whole path.

Defining the canyon floor width and wall distance functions...

I'll switch to canyon-relative coordinates: vertex offset u across the canyon, world x derived from the centerline plus u, so width stays constant and walls follow the path. The plateau sits beyond u=±70 but fog and low camera angle hide it; grid spacing around 1.5 units gives roughly 94 by 341 segments, about 32k vertices, which works okay for the cliff steepness with some terracing.

Now I'm refining the u-spacing to be nonuniform, denser near the canyon center using a power-curve mapping so detail concentrates where the camera is closest, with derivative checks at center versus edge to keep it smooth; bumping z to 400 segments gives roughly 64k vertices shared across two copies.

For the walls, I'm adding vertical noise to the displacement for erosion-like texture, then coloring vertices by height-strata bands (orange, red, tan, brown) with noise to break up uniformity. Since the steep walls are poorly resolved vertically for thin bands, I'm considering a custom shader via onBeforeCompile instead of plain vertex colors to get finer strata detail.

For lighting, I'm leaning toward MeshStandardMaterial with onBeforeCompile injections rather than a fully custom ShaderMaterial, since that gives built-in shadows, fog, and lighting support for free while still letting me inject a world-y varying for the strata coloring in the fragment shader—plus a directional light with a tight shadow frustum following the camera to get soft long shadows across the canyon.

I'm also weighing baked shadows via heightfield raymarching into vertex colors versus dynamic shadow maps. Baking would be cheap at runtime but costly at init and wouldn't account for boulders, so a camera-following shadow map is more robust for everything, including how a low sun angle interacts with the winding canyon walls to create asymmetric shadowing.

I'll add a hemisphere light for blue-tinted ambient shadows and bump the sun elevation slightly, with a gradient sky dome featuring a sun glow in magenta/orange near the horizon. For shadows, I'm setting up an orthographic shadow camera that follows the player, extending ±70 units in light space with a 2048 shadow map.

Checking that the light frustum's near/far range (0 to 600) and ±80 bounds cover the long shadows cast by the 45-unit-tall walls at a low 9° sun elevation, giving roughly 0.08 units per texel resolution — though grazing angles will still stretch shadow texels thin.

To fight acne I'll apply a normal bias around 0.5, and reduce shimmer by snapping the shadow camera's target to the light's texel grid using its right/up basis vectors rather than a naive world-space rounding. The far plane at 700 with light distance 350 should comfortably contain casters along the sun direction, even accounting for periodic tiling copies.

Shadow geometry at roughly 256k vertices across copies is manageable since each shadow camera does its own frustum culling per mesh bounds, and software rendering at 640×360 keeps fragment costs low. For fog, I want the color to match the sky near the horizon rather than straight blue, so I'm planning a custom hazy mauve tone that approximates the sky away from the sun, since the sky itself shifts from orange near the sun to bluish on the opposite side.

I'm considering whether to add real sun-direction scattering into the fog shader, but that requires world-position varyings I don't have for non-terrain materials like boulders, so I'll skip that complexity and stick with a simple exponential-squared fog using a density around 0.0065, which gives reasonable visibility falloff between 200 and 300 units.

For the sky, I'm designing a backside-shaded dome that ignores depth and fog, gradients from a horizon color through violet to deep zenith blue, with a sun glow computed as a sharpened dot-product power term for the orange-magenta disc, plus the fog color blending in below the horizon. I'm also reconsidering wall height since a 45-unit-tall canyon only 10 units away would block most of the sky from view, so I may need to lower the walls to keep the sky visible.

I'll vary plateau heights with noise and bump the camera pitch and FOV slightly. For the ground, I'm adding a sandy riverbed with a meandering channel of lighter sand, slight depth variation, and gentle undulation across the floor.

For texture detail, I'm generating a small random DataTexture to sample as procedural noise at multiple scales, using linear filtering and mipmaps to keep it smooth at low scale and avoid aliasing at high scale, blending strata and sand colors in the fragment shader based on height and slope.

For the shader injection with MeshStandardMaterial, I'm adding world-position and world-normal varyings in the vertex shader, computing world position manually after the vertex transform rather than relying on conditional built-in computation, and deriving the world normal from the object normal since transforms are translation-only.

For the fragment shader, I'm layering strata-based coloring using the vertex's y-position warped by low-frequency noise to tilt the bands, then sampling a palette across banded thickness to get a layered rock-strata look, swapped into the color fragment stage.

For the floor coloring I'm blending sandy tones with the strata based on slope and height, using the normal's y-component to separate flat ledges from steep walls, and adding a dusty blend on top surfaces so terraces pick up a soft sediment look.

Now I'm working out the terrain height function itself: distance from the canyon centerline plus low-frequency erosion noise, with asymmetric wall offsets on each side, then shaping the wall profile with a smoothed transition so it rises mostly vertically but with terraced steps rather than a gap between the floor and walls.

I'm quantizing the height into discrete terrace steps using a floor-plus-smoothstep trick on the fractional part, so each wall ends up with flat ledges roughly a meter wide separated by short steep risers, creating a stepped canyon-wall look rather than a smooth ramp.

I'm widening the ramp to span more distance, varying the step size with noise so the terraces aren't perfectly uniform, and adding alcove-like offsets plus small-scale roughness to the wall height so it doesn't look mechanical. Now I'm figuring out how to densify the mesh grid near the walls so the stair-stepping doesn't alias, mapping the parametric coordinate nonlinearly so resolution concentrates close to the wall boundary.

I'm not confident this is a documented gamma mismatch issue, so to be safe I'll just control fog myself through the sky shader rather than relying on the built-in fog chunk. Let me check the actual three.js source for how fog_fragment is ordered to confirm.

Since fog color is converted to sRGB output space without tonemapping, I realize my sky shader needs to output matching colors directly, bypassing the usual colorspace conversion since ShaderMaterial doesn't auto-convert.

I'm also thinking about matching sun glow between fog and sky - the horizon fog color could get slight sun scattering using a similar angular falloff based on view direction dotted with sun direction, applied consistently across terrain and sky materials. I'll build a shared helper that patches MeshStandardMaterial fog fragments with this glow effect, passing world position as a vertex varying so boulders and shrubs get the same treatment.

Writing sky shader code...

Writing fog fragment shader...

Checking that the fog density and camera far distance are tuned so the terrain's periodic copies get fully obscured at the plateau edge, confirming distances work out at the chosen density of 0.0075.

The mesh edges at the sides are far enough and fogged enough to not be visible from the floor viewpoint, and the sky haze color matches the far wall fade so the horizon blends seamlessly. Now I'm thinking through the boulder geometry using a low-detail icosahedron with noise displacement for flat-shaded rock shapes.

I'm deciding to skip instancing complexity and just place individual rock meshes directly on the terrain height, roughly a hundred total between the boulders and shrubs, with dead shrub branches built as procedurally generated merged cylinder geometry.

Using detail level 2 icosahedrons with noise displacement applied consistently per vertex position for smooth deformation, then computing vertex normals on the non-indexed geometry gives flat faceted shading, perfect for a rocky look. Shrubs get a dark brown-gray matte material without vertex colors, casting and receiving shadows despite minor flicker on small twigs. For placement, I'm using a seeded mulberry32 RNG to scatter positions across the floor width and along the period length.

Boulders near the wall bases can extend slightly beyond the period boundary since their radius is small, which just overlaps harmlessly with the next tile's boulders at the seam — equivalent to how the previous tile's boulder would overlap into this one. For height accuracy, I'll use the same terrain height function for both camera positioning and mesh vertices so they stay consistent, and since the floor bumps are small amplitude and low frequency, minor discrepancies at vertex boundaries won't be noticeable. I also need to make sure boulders and shrubs never spawn directly in the camera's drifting path—since the camera weaves side to side along the track, I should exclude placement within a buffer radius around that drift curve so obstacles don't visually clip through the camera.

For the terrain itself, I'm defining the floor height as noise-based bumps combined with a carved river channel: the river follows a sinuous centerline that shifts across the width, and the depth falls off smoothly with distance from that centerline to form banks. Now I'm working out how the canyon walls blend into this floor height smoothly, using a distance-based falloff that's asymmetric on each side of the channel.

I'm checking the slope of the sine-based centerline curve, since combining multiple harmonics gives a max derivative around 1.5 — that's roughly a 56° twist, which risks distorting the sheared coordinate grid too aggressively and could cause the camera to clip into canyon walls. Writing noise functions...
